Reviewed service models/shared responsibility, organization and account boundaries, control/data planes, region/zone/failure models, resilience/RTO/RPO, IAM/network boundaries, common workload building blocks, pricing/telemetry, every example, exercise, and interview answer.

Corrected the misleading “cloud project” definition: Google Cloud projects are fundamental resource/policy containers; AWS Organizations organizes accounts and “project” is context-specific. Added explicit Google Cloud versus AWS hierarchy distinctions and NIST cloud definition source coverage. Corrected cross-provider Well-Architected pillar coverage: Azure workload guidance has five core pillars, while AWS has six including Sustainability. Refreshed date-stamped provider sources to 2026-11-20.

All 5 supplied inventory groups and 217 named entries, stated comparisons and exclusions were checked against the lesson set; no unresolved factual or scope gaps remain. All 9 lessons remain drafts pending course-wide promotion.

auditFindings.scope: Microsoft Azure architecture identity networking compute and data services (t09-010)
auditFindings.status: full claim and frozen-inventory audit complete for all 10 lessons
findings: Audited all 10 lessons and six manifest inventories against current Microsoft Learn documentation for Azure Resource Manager, Bicep, policy, Entra ID, RBAC, networking/private connectivity, compute, Functions, storage, databases, messaging, monitoring, backup and cost. Checked every assigned inventory name, example, failure boundary, lifecycle statement, exercise and interview answer.

Corrected ARM complete-mode guidance: it deletes omitted resources at supported resource-group scope, is not recommended and is gradually deprecated; deployment stacks are recommended for intentional deletions. Refreshed Azure snapshot dates. Updated Redis creation restrictions for July 2026 changes (eligible existing tenants remain allowed through retirement), and made Managed Redis preview limitations explicit. Confirmed Functions in-process support ended 2026-11-10, and Flex Consumption remains Microsoft’s recommended Functions serverless plan.
All six inventory groups and the source-backed accuracy facts were checked. No unresolved factual or scope gaps remain. All 10 lessons remain drafts pending course-wide promotion.

auditFindings.scope: AWS architecture identity networking compute and data services (t09-011)
auditFindings.status: full claim and frozen-inventory audit complete for all 9 lessons
findings: Audited all nine lessons and supplied inventories against current AWS official documentation, including IAM policy evaluation, Organizations, VPC, EKS/ECS, Lambda, S3, RDS, DynamoDB, queues/events, CloudWatch/CloudTrail/Config, backup, cost, and Well-Architected. Reviewed examples, failure scenarios, practice solutions and interview answers.

Corrected the Lambda Managed Instances synchronous invocation timeout: current AWS guidance permits up to 30 minutes for synchronous calls, 90 minutes for eligible asynchronous/event-source calls (with Amazon MQ and DocumentDB remaining 15 minutes), and keeps initialization at 15 minutes. The prior fact incorrectly stated synchronous calls remained at 15 minutes.

Updated AWS Well-Architected coverage for its November 16, 2026 major revision: six pillar whitepapers are consolidated, Cloud Foundations is now a separate organization-wide section, and the six workload pillars remain under Cloud Workloads. Checked RDS Multi-AZ instance versus cluster distinctions. No unresolved factual or frozen-inventory gaps remain; lessons remain drafts.

auditFindings.scope: Kubernetes workloads configuration scheduling and networking (t09-008)
auditFindings.status: full claim and frozen-inventory audit complete for all 11 lessons
findings: Audited all 11 lessons and seven manifest inventories against official Kubernetes documentation and release notes. Reviewed API objects/reconciliation, lifecycle and probes, controllers/rollouts, Services/Ingress/Gateway, storage/configuration, resource accounting, scheduling/autoscaling/disruption, security/RBAC/admission/extensions, examples, exercises and interview answers.

Confirmed v1.37.1 remains the latest listed upstream release on 2026-11-20. Corrected a conflation in the pod resource explanation: the `.spec.resources` CPU/memory/hugepages API is Beta since v1.34 and enabled by default in v1.37, while Pod-level resource managers are a distinct Beta feature in v1.37 that is disabled by default and requires its feature gate. Updated the snapshot date throughout.

Checked v1.37 metrics API/HPA scale-to-zero/DRA changes, v1.35 in-place resize, v1.36 user namespaces and storage features, and implementation dependencies such as CSI, CNI, Gateway controllers, metrics adapters and feature gates. No unresolved factual or assigned-inventory gaps remain; lessons remain drafts.

auditFindings.scope: t07-026, t07-027, t12-009 and five linked performance concept additions
auditFindings.status: lesson-level factual and inventory review complete; global promotion gate remains closed
findings: Completed claim and assigned-inventory review for all 37 new lesson units across browser persistence/offline work, end-to-end browser request lifecycle, and integrated cross-stack performance. Per-lesson source evidence and claim inventories are recorded on each lesson ledger entry.
Reviewed and recorded five existing concept lessons changed to connect performance across ASP.NET Core, EF Core, React, React framework deployment, and system-design foundations.

No material factual corrections were required after the source and consistency pass. The global draft promotion gate remains false because separate curriculum-level content-quality findings remain open.

evidence.claim: Big O is an upper-bound notation; Theta expresses matching asymptotic upper and lower bounds.
For two balanced recursive halves and constant combine work, T(n)=2T(n/2)+Theta(1) solves to Theta(n).
Balanced recursive maximum finding has logarithmic call-stack depth.
An iterative scan can use Theta(1) auxiliary state.
evidence.section: Space analysis; direct algorithm state count

evidence.claim: Algorithm analysis requires an input-size parameter and a resource/cost measure.

evidence.claim: Amortized analysis bounds costs over operation sequences without requiring an input probability distribution.
Asymptotic notation is independent of whether the function describes best, average, or worst-case cost.
Big O, Big Omega, Big Theta, little o, and little omega represent upper, lower, tight, and strict bounds.
Recursive cost models require recurrences and base values.
Iteration, recursion trees, substitution, and the Master theorem are distinct recurrence-analysis approaches.
The Master theorem applies only to a restricted divide-and-conquer form and its hypotheses.
Aggregate, accounting, and potential are amortized-analysis methods.

evidence.claim: Numeric algorithm input is often measured by bit length when arithmetic cost depends on representation size.
Running time counts operations under a model and is not identical to machine-dependent wall-clock time.
Auxiliary space conventionally means additional working storage, with output treatment stated explicitly.
Best case is the minimum cost over inputs of a fixed size.
Average-case cost is an expectation under a stated input distribution.
Worst-case cost is the maximum over inputs of a fixed size.
Amortized cost bounds sequence totals rather than each operation independently.
Dynamic-array append can cost Theta(n) during a resize but append-only total work is O(n) under geometric doubling.

Big O is an upper bound and does not specify an analysis case.

evidence.claim: Big O formalizes an eventual asymptotic upper bound with positive constants c and n0.
Big Omega formalizes an eventual asymptotic lower bound.
Big Theta holds when a function is both O and Omega of the comparison function.
Little o is a strict upper-growth relation and can be defined by every positive constant bound eventually.
Little omega is the strict lower-growth counterpart.
These five notations are a common set, not a complete inventory of all asymptotic relations.
evidence.section: Chapter 13, asymptotic relations including asymptotic equivalence

evidence.claim: Notation describes a function bound and is not synonymous with worst-case analysis.
If a function is both O(g) and Omega(g), it is Theta(g).
For T(n)=3n^2+5n+2, an eventual O(n^2) bound holds with c=4 and n0=6.
The same polynomial is Theta(n^2) by matching upper and lower bounds.
This polynomial is o(n^3) but not o(n^2), as shown by ratio limits.
A 7n log n - 4n function is Theta(n log n) for sufficiently large n.
5n^2 is not O(n) because the ratio to n is unbounded.
Strict and non-strict asymptotic relations are not interchangeable.

evidence.claim: The current MDN index includes ::column, ::scroll-button(), and ::search-text.

::search-text represents user-agent find-in-page matches, is optional to implement, and may combine with :current for the focused match.

No unresolved in-scope omissions remain; draft status is retained pending curriculum-wide completion.

evidence.claim: DNS is a distributed hierarchical domain-name system; resolvers cache responses subject to DNS TTL information.
A DNS address result does not authenticate the application service identity; service identity verification is a separate TLS/application check.
TCP provides a reliable, ordered byte stream rather than application message boundaries; applications need their own framing.

TLS 1.3 is specified by RFC 9846 (July 2026), which obsoletes RFC 8446 while retaining version 1.3 and backward compatibility; it forbids KeyShare reuse across connections and TLS 1.0/1.1 negotiation.
TLS provides confidentiality, integrity, and peer authentication when the protocol is configured and identity validation is performed; mutual client authentication is optional.
HTTP/1.1 uses persistent connections; requests on a connection are sequential and pipelining can suffer application-level head-of-line blocking.
RFC 9931 (March 2026) adds security requirements for optimistic HTTP/1.1 protocol transitions and CONNECT handling, including protections against forwarding untrusted data before acceptance.
HTTP/2 allows concurrent exchanges on one connection and compresses fields, but TCP packet loss can stall all active transactions sharing that TCP connection.
HTTP/3 maps HTTP semantics over QUIC and uses QUIC stream multiplexing; loss on one stream does not block progress on other streams, while congestion control is shared across the connection.
RFC 6455 WebSocket has an opening handshake followed by framed two-way communication; RFC 8441 separately defines WebSocket bootstrapping over HTTP/2 with extended CONNECT.
WebSocket protocol support does not itself supply application authorization, durable replay, or fan-out policy.

The WHATWG EventSource API opens a server-to-client event stream over HTTP and reconnects after closure; Last-Event-ID supports resumption only when the server has and returns corresponding event history.
The lesson’s HTTP/2, HTTP/3, WebSocket, and SSE comparison accurately distinguishes transport/protocol behavior from application authorization, replay, backpressure, and fan-out responsibilities.

evidence.claim: G-Counter uses one non-negative component per known replica; each replica increments its own component, queries sum all components, and merge takes component-wise maximum.
A single scalar merged by max loses concurrent increments, and a sum merge is not idempotent; vector components preserve per-replica monotonicity.
The classic construction assumes known replica membership and no numeric overflow.
The component merge is associative, commutative, idempotent, and monotone, yielding convergence after all updates are represented in exchanged states.
A G-Counter cannot decrement by reducing a component; doing so breaks monotonicity.
A G-Counter alone cannot enforce a hard business quota under concurrent increments; a coordinated or rights-based design is needed.
Replica identity reuse without preserving the prior component can lose count information.
evidence.section: Derived from per-replica component and known-membership invariant in §3.1.2

evidence.claim: The lesson distinguishes compact component vectors from the G-Set unique-event alternative for unknown membership.

evidence.claim: PN-Counter represents positive and negative operations with two grow-only per-replica vectors P and N.
The visible value is sum(P) minus sum(N).
Each replica increments only its own component in P for increment and N for decrement; merge is component-wise maximum for both vectors.
The state-based construction relies on monotone components and stable replica identity; state exchange converges under the CRDT assumptions.
The visible result may become negative when disconnected replicas decrement based on stale reads.
PN-Counter does not itself enforce non-negativity, quotas, or conditional decrement invariants.
Safe bounded counters require additional rights/coordination construction, not ordinary PN-Counter behavior.
Metadata and local availability trade against fresh global reads and invariant enforcement.

evidence.claim: Each add creates a unique tag for the element; a remove targets only tags observed at its source.

Safe metadata compaction needs proof that stale messages/states cannot reintroduce removed tags; optimized constructions have distinct assumptions.
Unlike 2P-Set, OR-Set permits re-addition after removal with a new tag.
CRDT convergence does not guarantee a product’s desired conflict policy; add-wins may be wrong when removal must win.
Metadata may grow with add/removal history if not safely compacted.

evidence.claim: Bounded-load hashing models keys as balls and servers as bins, assigns by consistent-hash order, and forwards from a full bin to the next non-full bin.
With m balls, n bins, and parameter c>1, capacity is at most ceil(c*m/n).
For m=n and c=2, the maximum load is at most 2 and expected movement per single key/server update is constant.
General expected movement bounds depend on epsilon=c-1 and are relative to unavoidable lower bounds.
The paper assumes updates are handled one at a time with time to restore invariant before the next update.
The bound applies to key count, not automatically to bytes, CPU, or request rate.
A hot key can still overload a single owner even if key counts meet the bound.

evidence.claim: Cap parameter trades load balance against movement and forwarding.
This theorem is not a blanket guarantee for arbitrary weighted heterogeneous servers or replicas.

evidence.claim: Maglev is a network load balancer using per-service backend pools and health checks; backend health is maintained separately from hashing.
Maglev assigns each backend a deterministic preference permutation over table slots and fills the lookup table in rounds.
Prime table size and offset/skip permutations give each backend a traversal of slots.
With equal turn frequency, each backend receives floor(M/N) or ceil(M/N) entries, differing by at most one.
Runtime selection is hash then table lookup.
Maglev emphasizes even load balancing more than minimal disruption compared with some ring/rendezvous schemes.
Rebuilding the table after backend set changes can remap entries; a larger table reduces disruption but raises memory/build costs.
Paper supports weights by altering relative backend turn frequency but does not specify implementation details.
Connection tracking helps preserve established flow affinity while mappings change, subject to failures and implementation behavior.
Maglev does not replicate application data or provide application-level session state.

evidence.claim: Cassandra read repair occurs during a read when replicas involved at the requested consistency level disagree; the coordinator reconciles data and repairs only stale replicas involved in the read.
evidence.section: Read repair; read consistency and read repair

evidence.claim: The read response may not be the globally newest data when the requested consistency level does not involve all replicas.
Cassandra blocking read repair supports monotonic quorum reads, preventing a subsequent quorum read from going older under the documented failed-quorum-write scenario.
Cassandra BLOCKING waits for repair writes to reach the requested consistency level and does not provide partition-level write atomicity for partial-partition reads.
Cassandra NONE reconciles response data without repair writes, preserving partition-level write atomicity but not monotonic quorum reads.
Read repair can break partition write atomicity when a multi-row partition write is read at more granular row scope.
Cassandra 4.0 introduced table-level `read_repair` options and removed background `read_repair_chance` and `dclocal_read_repair_chance` settings.

evidence.claim: Independent additions may merge only when the selected set datatype defines compatible add semantics; removals need an explicit conflict rule such as observed-remove tags.
Hard invariants such as unique ownership or limited inventory require a defined authoritative transaction/coordination or rights-allocation path.
Replaying operations safely requires stable operation identity/idempotency and, where needed, causal/version metadata.
Testing reordered, duplicated, and reconnecting operations is appropriate for eventual/replicated workflows with asynchronous delivery.
Workload estimates should state assumptions and quantify average/peak/burst load, concurrency, payload, and retention.
Authoritative state and derived representations need an explicit refresh/rebuild/reconciliation contract.
After a timeout, a remote write may have succeeded; retry safety requires an idempotency key or outcome verification.
Dependency degradation should preserve critical behavior and be observed through latency/error/queue-age and trace signals.
Scaling choices should be driven by the constrained resource and measured evidence such as saturation, tail latency, queue age, or cache cost.
Edge cases should cover duplicate requests, slow consumers, stale cache, zone/provider outage, schema rollout, tenant isolation, and backup restoration.
The exercises do not imply one architecture for every workload; answers require stating assumptions and evidence.
The worked solution distinguishes convergent user-authored data from serialized payment/inventory invariants.

evidence.claim: A strong interview answer starts from user outcomes and invariants, then makes workload, authority, failure, security, and observability assumptions explicit.
A timeout leaves a potentially unknown remote outcome; idempotency or verification is required before unsafe retry.
Tenant isolation and abuse/privacy belong in request/data-boundary design.
Observability claims should connect objectives to measurable signals and recovery.
Linearizability, sequential consistency, and eventual consistency answer distinct visibility/order questions.
Read-your-writes is a session guarantee and not global visibility.
Lamport, vector, and HLC have distinct causality/concurrency/physical-time tradeoffs.
State-based and operation-based CRDTs depend on different merge/delivery assumptions.
Consistent and rendezvous hashing assign keys to members using different lookup structures; neither solves hot-key skew by itself.
Consensus replicates agreement on a value/log, while 2PC coordinates atomic commit across participants and may block; they are distinct.
A response lost after commit requires idempotency/status recovery rather than assuming rollback.
A single tenant can create hot-key or resource contention; isolation and partitioning decisions require workload evidence.
Queue depth alone may not represent user-perceived delay; queue age/latency and end-to-end traces help reveal delayed work.
Mixed-version/schema deployment should preserve compatibility and support rollback or expand/contract sequencing.
Multi-region conflict handling depends on operation semantics; some operations merge while invariants may require coordination or one authority.

evidence.claim: Redis embeds Lua 5.1 for server-side scripting and exposes script keys/arguments through KEYS and ARGV.
Script execution is atomic relative to other Redis commands on the executing server, and blocks those commands while it runs.
Running logic near the data can reduce network round trips for read/decision/write sequences.
evidence.verdict: supported as a design benefit, not a latency guarantee

evidence.claim: Every accessed key must be declared as a key argument; Redis Cluster requires multi-key operations/scripts to use one hash slot.
EVALSHA depends on Redis script-cache presence, and applications must recover if a script is absent.
Redis Functions were added in Redis 7 and provide server-managed libraries that are persisted and replicated.
Redis Functions and Eval scripts both have atomic, blocking execution semantics.
A slow script stalls other work on that Redis server; after writes have occurred it cannot be safely interrupted with SCRIPT KILL.
Redis script atomicity does not provide one transaction spanning Redis and SQL Server or arbitrary cluster shards.
evidence.section: Cluster key-slot scope; Redis transaction scope

evidence.claim: WATCH with MULTI/EXEC implements optimistic conflict detection and clients must handle aborted/retried transactions.
A retry-safe reservation requires application logic to store and enforce a stable reservation/idempotency identifier.
evidence.verdict: supported as a condition; lesson makes enforcement explicit

evidence.claim: Inventory authority, expiry, and reconciliation with a durable order store remain separate design decisions.
This reference is conceptual; exact implementation features and behavior vary by product, version, configuration, and deployment.
evidence.section: EVAL scripts and Redis Functions version/lifecycle differences
evidence.verdict: supported; the lesson labels product/version boundaries and cites the current official profile or specification.

evidence.claim: Starting Redis 7.4, Redis can evict scripts loaded by EVAL/EVAL_RO when its script cache reaches a certain size, so EVALSHA callers must handle cache misses.
evidence.section: EVAL note on script cache eviction since 7.4
evidence.verdict: supported; lesson includes the version boundary and recovery case.

evidence.claim: HLS delivers live and on-demand media through playlists and media resources over HTTP infrastructure, including web servers and CDNs.
A Multivariant/Master Playlist lists available variants and rendition groups; a Media Playlist describes media segments.

HLS classic RFC 8216 is an August 2017 Informational document describing protocol version 7, not a complete description of all current profiles.
evidence.section: RFC status; Apple maintained authoring specification

evidence.claim: Adaptive switching depends on compatible renditions, timing, codecs, and playlist metadata rather than bitrate entries alone.
Low-Latency HLS is a coordinated origin, packager, CDN, and player feature; reducing segment duration alone does not define the full protocol behavior.
HLS encryption/content protection feature behavior depends on key format and target platform; Apple authoring profile specifies FairPlay requirements.
Media encryption is not equivalent to E2EE because the streaming service generally participates in key delivery, entitlement, or packaging.
evidence.section: Client key fetch and content protection

evidence.claim: MPEG-DASH and HLS both use HTTP adaptive streaming but have distinct manifest/profile interoperability requirements.
CMAF can support shared media packaging workflows across compatible HLS/DASH profiles but does not make every manifest, codec, protection system, or player interchangeable.
evidence.section: DASH CMAF part; HLS CMAF support

evidence.claim: Live streaming design should measure glass-to-glass latency, playback stalls, and recovery rather than infer latency from segment duration alone.
